fields.description: We are designing a Swiss day-trip planner that turns a departure point, time window, interests and mobility preferences into executable weekend options. A constraint engine checks curated routes against transport and weather data; users compare plans, save one and refine future suggestions through feedback.
fields.innovation: Residents often spend more time choosing an outing than enjoying it, because ideas, transport, opening hours and personal constraints sit in separate tools. Our core innovation is a feasibility-first recommendation process: it filters curated day trips against a return deadline, walking limits and known conditions before ranking for interests and variety. Existing cards and previously visited places inform the result without turning unverified discounts into promises. The planned difference from generic search or itinerary chatbots is a small set of executable, explained alternatives rather than an unconstrained list. We will test that difference against users' current planning methods. Our proposed lead is a maintained local content base, distribution through resident communities and consented feedback that improves matching. The TREK-based code will follow AGPL; we do not claim a patent or exclusive ownership of upstream software.
fields.technology: The concept is at product-design stage, with open-source TREK identified as a possible foundation; its existing features are not a completed startup MVP. The proposed web/PWA product combines React, NestJS and shared validation with a new template and constraint module. Transport and weather adapters provide dated evidence; missing prices or stale conditions stay explicit. Initial scope is one departure city, 20-30 curated templates and two languages. Over six weeks we plan interviews and manual recommendations, then preference input, feasibility checks, saved plans and a limited paid trial. Medium-term work would add feedback-based diversification and partner distribution only if repeat use is demonstrated. Risks include data access, inaccurate availability, content upkeep, privacy and weak retention. We will validate source terms, private sessions, return deadlines and offline freshness before expanding. We plan to add an OJP 2.0 adapter to TREK's existing transit module, mapping Swiss journey queries to its common itinerary format for connection and return-time checks. API keys stay server-side; feed access and coverage remain to be validated.
fields.team: I am Leo (Yudong) Zhong, a solo founder based in Zurich with a Swiss B permit. I have over five years of experience shipping production AI, including perception and tracking systems deployed on the XPeng MONA M03. I also built EuroJobHunter, a live job-matching SaaS using multi-provider LLM orchestration, autonomous pipelines and MCP tools, and won third prize in Intel's AI PC Innovation Application Competition for an on-device agent. I hold a master's degree from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. I will lead product, software delivery, data integration and initial customer interviews. These projects show production engineering and independent delivery; they are not tourism traction. I will recruit a local content verifier and test distribution with resident communities before considering an employer-sales role. I currently have no co-founder or confirmed tourism partner. Hiring will follow pilot evidence and budget, with roles and commitments documented explicitly.
fields.market: Our first customer hypothesis is a Swiss resident without a car who wants practical weekend ideas; newly arrived residents and people hosting visitors are candidate segments. They currently use search, social media, tourism websites, maps, SBB and general AI assistants. We aim to win through verified feasibility and lower decision effort, not a larger attraction catalogue. The initial serviceable market must be sized from [VERIFIED BEACHHEAD RESIDENT OR PARTNER COUNT], reachable users and tested annual spend; no national TAM has been validated. Available transport and weather data make a focused prototype possible now, but do not prove demand. No customer interviews, users or revenue exist for this tourism concept yet. We plan 15 resident interviews, manual recommendations across two weekends and tests of actual outings, repeat use and willingness to pay. Findings, including rejection reasons and free alternatives, will determine the segment before scale-up.
fields.impact: We aim to contribute to SDG 11 through practical access to local experiences and to SDG 12 through informed travel choices. Residents and local operators could benefit if verified recommendations lead to outings that would otherwise be abandoned or poorly matched. KPIs will include actual outings, repeat use, planning time and transport mode relative to each user's stated alternative. No impact results or carbon savings are established yet. At scale we will estimate reach from active users and observed adoption, not downloads. Negative effects include induced travel, concentration at recommended places, digital exclusion and data-processing energy. We will diversify suggestions, preserve user choice and avoid unverified environmental claims.
fields.business: We plan to test a direct-to-consumer model: CHF 5-9 for a detailed outing and CHF 9-15 per month only if repeat use supports a subscription. Employer distribution is a separate hypothesis, not a confirmed customer channel. Initial acquisition will use resident communities and partner referrals; paid advertising will wait until contribution per customer is understood. This tourism venture has no users or revenue; funding and monthly costs still need confirmation. Proposed milestones are problem interviews, manual trials, a one-city MVP and initial paid purchases within six weeks. We will track content hours, API and hosting costs, support and acquisition per buyer. Main risks are low leisure willingness to pay, free substitutes, seasonal use and high upkeep. Expansion depends on actual outings, repeat demand and a credible path to covering direct costs.

fields.description: We are designing an adaptive Swiss travel assistant that checks an existing itinerary against weather, transport and user constraints. It identifies affected activities, preserves locked bookings and proposes explained alternatives. Travelers compare changes and explicitly confirm a new plan version.
fields.innovation: A trip can become impractical after a weather change, delayed connection or reduced walking capacity. Travelers must reconcile several information sources while remembering fixed bookings. Our core innovation is constraint-preserving adaptation: identify the affected time window, keep immovable commitments and suggest a small set of feasible replacements with visible trade-offs. Unlike a fresh AI itinerary, a proposal is tied to the original plan, evidence freshness and a specific version, and cannot silently alter external reservations. We will compare its usefulness with manual replanning and existing assistants. The intended lead is reliable change handling, curated local alternatives and distribution through travel-service partners. Code derived from TREK remains under AGPL; defensibility must come from maintained operations and validated user value, not an invented patent or proprietary claim over upstream features.
fields.technology: This is a design-stage concept, not a deployed adaptive service. TREK offers existing itinerary, reservation, weather, transport and offline components; we propose a new impact-assessment and plan-version module. Structured constraints govern feasibility, while AI may explain results without inventing operational facts. The first release would cover one region, low-risk sightseeing, weather checks and user-triggered changes; transport-event automation depends on verified feed coverage. The six-week roadmap is interviews and historical cases, manual adjustments and data tests, then locked activities, proposals, versioned confirmation and a small trial. Later work may add opted-in notifications and agency tools. Technical risks are stale or incomplete feeds, timezone errors and conflicting updates. We will test idempotent confirmation, privacy and fail-safe retention of the original plan; we do not offer mountain-safety decisions or automatic rebooking. We plan to add an OJP 2.0 adapter to TREK's existing transit module, mapping Swiss journey queries to its common itinerary format for connection and return-time checks. API keys stay server-side; feed access and coverage remain to be validated.

Switzerland recorded 43.9 million hotel nights in 2025, which is context, not our addressable customer count. We must establish [VERIFIED ELIGIBLE TRIP OR AGENCY COUNT] and the incidence of meaningful changes before estimating market revenue. Alternatives include weather apps, SBB, tourism websites, manual agency support and AI planners. Customers would choose us if preserving bookings and comparing feasible changes saves measurable replanning effort. No customer interviews, users or revenue exist for this tourism concept yet. fields.description: We are designing a Swiss travel-ticket comparison tool that maps a fixed itinerary and passenger eligibility to a limited set of ticket combinations. A versioned rules engine checks coverage, retrieves available quotes and explains estimated cost, flexibility and unresolved conditions before official purchase.
fields.innovation: Travelers can struggle to compare passes, individual tickets, discounts and booking restrictions across an itinerary. Our innovation is an explainable coverage model: each product is mapped to each journey segment with eligibility, validity and uncertainty, then combinations are compared under the same passenger and flexibility assumptions. This avoids presenting a cheaper but materially different journey as savings. Unknown coverage is excluded from verified cheapest-option claims. The planned advantage over a fare lookup or chatbot is transparent multi-product reasoning and reviewable assumptions. We will test a narrow product whitelist against official purchase conditions and human experts before extending it. Our lead would depend on a maintained rules library, verified edge cases and agency distribution. We will comply with TREK's AGPL requirements and data-source terms; we claim neither a patent nor guaranteed lowest prices.
fields.technology: The product is currently a design-stage proposal using TREK's itinerary, transport and cost display as potential foundations. We propose a ticket-rule module, coverage matrix, bounded combination solver and quote adapters. OJP Fare is a candidate data service, not an already integrated source; access, limits and product coverage must be tested, and its quotes are non-binding. The initial scope is fixed itineraries and a small verified set of products, with explicit unknowns and official purchase links. Over six weeks we plan data checks, manually reviewed cases, rule implementation, comparison pages and limited paid reviews. Medium-term work would add products only with a sustainable update process. Risks are changing conditions, incomplete quotes, eligibility errors and user expectations. Tests will cover validity dates, overlapping benefits, missing fares and stale results; the MVP will not sell tickets or manage refunds. We plan to add an OJP 2.0 adapter to TREK's existing transit module, mapping Swiss journey queries to its common itinerary format for connection and return-time checks. API keys stay server-side; feed access and coverage remain to be validated.

fields.description: We are designing a Swiss microtrip planner for conference and business travelers. It works backward from a required return time to match nearby experiences with transport, walking and luggage constraints. Users receive explained options, shorter alternatives and dated return information.
fields.innovation: Business and conference travelers may have a useful gap in their schedule but cannot easily judge what fits before the next commitment. Our innovation is deadline-first planning: work backward from a required arrival, reserve explicit buffers and match only experiences with sufficient usable time. Luggage needs, opening conditions and shortened routes are part of feasibility, not afterthoughts. We will compare this approach with event guides, maps, hotel advice and general itinerary tools. The planned advantage is reliable scope and transparent return assumptions rather than an assurance that no one will miss a flight. Our intended lead is reusable venue-area content and distribution through event organizers or business hotels. TREK-derived code follows AGPL; we do not claim patented routing or exclusive upstream capabilities. Channel relationships and verified execution must establish the lead.
fields.technology: The concept is at design stage, with TREK's itinerary, maps, transit and calendar features as candidate foundations. We propose an event-profile module, availability windows, reverse-time feasibility and return rechecks. Initial scope is one venue area and 10-15 verified short routes; manual time input avoids access to full corporate calendars. Over six weeks we plan organizer interviews, local checks and manual recommendations, then mobile entry pages, time constraints and an event or hotel trial. Medium-term work could add opt-in reminders and companion itineraries if demand is verified. Risks include timetable gaps, delays, unknown luggage storage and timezone errors. The service will use the user's explicit arrival deadline, not certify airport processing time or guarantee flight connections. Tests cover shortened windows, return changes, session privacy and failed notifications. We plan to add an OJP 2.0 adapter to TREK's existing transit module, mapping Swiss journey queries to its common itinerary format for connection and return-time checks. API keys stay server-side; feed access and coverage remain to be validated.

Data and browser distribution make small trials possible, but business context alone does not prove a work-productivity benefit. fields.description: We are designing a car-free Swiss outdoor planner that joins public transport, verified low-intensity walking routes and feasible returns. It checks time windows, transfer walks and exit options, and provides a saved route with dated conditions. Initial scope excludes safety-critical mountain activities.
fields.innovation: An outdoor route and its public-transport access are often planned separately, especially when the walk ends somewhere different from its start. Our innovation is joint feasibility: verify outward and return connections, include access walks, allow for rest and buffers, and explain shorter exits. Missing route or condition data is treated as unknown rather than evidence of safety. We will benchmark against SwitzerlandMobility, maps, SBB and users' manual planning. The intended difference is a complete, limited-scope outing whose transport and route assumptions are traceable. Our lead would come from lawful route content, maintained connections, field checks and accommodation or community distribution. TREK's existing road routing is not a validated outdoor engine, and AGPL obligations remain. We do not claim a patent, universal route safety or guaranteed returns.

We would reuse TREK maps, GPX display, itinerary, weather, transit and offline capabilities, then add verified route segments, exit nodes and a connection-feasibility module. GeoAdmin data and transit services are candidates whose terms, coverage and limits require testing. The first release would contain 10-15 low-intensity, daylight routes in one region. Six-week work covers interviews, lawful content sourcing, field checks, route/transport matching, mobile saved plans and actual trials. Later expansion could add seasonal packages or hotel distribution. Risks include missing closures, inaccurate duration, licensing and stale return data. We will test access walks, transport calendars, buffers, exits and snapshot age. The product will not evaluate mountaineering, avalanche or other safety-critical conditions. We plan to add an OJP 2.0 adapter to TREK's existing transit module, mapping Swiss journey queries to its common itinerary format for connection and return-time checks. API keys stay server-side; feed access and coverage remain to be validated.

fields.description: We are designing a destination-service tool that matches visitors with suitable local experiences using interests, access constraints and dated operator availability. Our innovation is an auditable matching and measurement workflow: filter for visitor constraints, use dated operator statements, manage exposure and distinguish recommendation interest from actual visits. Unknown capacity is not labeled as low crowding, and paid promotion cannot override hard needs. We will test whether this improves on static destination lists, campaign placement and manual coordination. The intended lead is cooperative operating relationships, verified local content and credible outcome measurement. At first we will not claim predictive crowd models or causal congestion reduction. TREK-derived code follows AGPL; defensibility must come from maintained partnerships and learning, not unproven patents or control of public data.
fields.technology: This concept is at design stage, without confirmed destination partners or a deployed visitor-flow system. The six-week roadmap starts with budget and data-owner interviews, manual availability and recommendations, then role-based tools, dated states and a limited trial. Medium-term work would require sustained cooperation before prediction or broader procurement. We will test status expiry, permissions and consent; no continuous visitor tracking is planned. Small pilots will report descriptive outcomes rather than unsupported causal claims. fields.description: We are designing a group-outing planner that privately collects dates, starting points, budgets and walking preferences, then finds feasible shared options. It explains trade-offs, supports versioned voting and turns an explicitly confirmed choice into a collaborative itinerary.
fields.innovation: Group outings often stall while organizers reconcile dates, departure locations, budgets and comfort needs in chats. Our core innovation is a private-preference feasibility workflow that finds shared options before voting and explains why no common plan exists. Users can compare fairness objectives, such as reducing the longest individual journey versus total group travel, rather than accept an unexplained ranking. Changes create a new candidate version, so old votes cannot silently endorse a different plan. We will compare this with chat, date polls and existing group-planning tools. Our planned lead is trusted organizer workflows, reusable regional content and distribution to recurring groups. TREK collaboration is a foundation, not the new constraint solver. AGPL obligations remain, and we do not claim proprietary ownership of upstream voting or a patent on fairness.
fields.technology: The product is at design stage with no group trials completed. We propose to build on TREK membership, chat, polls, costs and itinerary features, adding private preferences, bounded option enumeration, fairness explanations and confirmed-decision versions. Initial scope is three to eight people, a few dates and curated regional day activities; manual availability avoids access to complete calendars. The six-week roadmap is organizer interviews and manual group tasks, then invitations, privacy, feasible options, versioned voting and real trials. Medium-term work may focus on corporate organizers if that segment pays. Risks are low member response, no shared feasible plan, stale transport and preference exposure. We will test invitation scope, withdrawal, unknown budgets, old votes and duplicate confirmation. The MVP will neither collect money nor book external activities automatically. We plan to add an OJP 2.0 adapter to TREK's existing transit module, mapping Swiss journey queries to its common itinerary format for connection and return-time checks. API keys stay server-side; feed access and coverage remain to be validated.
